examples.question_text:
A class records its favourite outdoor activities.

| Activity | Number of students |
| --- | --- |
| Cycling | 9 |
| Swimming | 12 |
| Walking | 6 |

Choose a suitable graph for comparing the numbers. Explain your choice.
examples.solution_text: Use a **column graph**. The activities are categories, and separate column heights make their numbers easy to compare.

examples.question_text:
A gardener records a plant's height at the end of four consecutive weeks.

| Week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Height (cm) | 8 | 11 | 15 | 18 |

Choose a suitable graph for showing how the height changes over time. Explain your choice.
examples.solution_text: Use a **line graph**. Place the weeks in order on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical axis. Joining consecutive measurements shows how the height changes over time.

examples.question_text:
Students count birds at three named parks: Riverside $6$, Hilltop $10$ and Lakeside $8$.

A student suggests joining the three counts on a line graph. Explain why this is inappropriate for comparing the parks, and suggest a suitable graph.
examples.solution_text:
The park names are categories. A line would suggest meaningful values between park names, but there is no halfway park between Riverside and Hilltop.

Use a **column graph** with a separate column for each park.

examples.question_text:
A class records its favourite fruit.

| Fruit | Number of students |
| --- | --- |
| Apple | 12 |
| Banana | 6 |
| Orange | 6 |

Which is more useful for showing each fruit's share of all choices: a column graph or a sector graph? Explain your choice.
examples.solution_text: Use a **sector graph**. The whole circle represents all choices, and each sector represents one fruit's share of the whole.

examples.question_text:
A shop sells $150$ pencils, $230$ pens and $320$ markers in a week.

A proposed picture graph uses one carefully drawn picture for every item sold. Explain why a column graph would be more appropriate for comparing these sales.
examples.solution_text:
The picture graph would require hundreds of drawings, making it slow to draw and read.

A **column graph** compares the sales using three columns. An even vertical scale in steps of $50$, from $0$ to $350$, would fit the largest count.

examples.question_text:
A library records how many books each visitor borrows.

| Books borrowed | Number of visitors |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | 120 |
| 2 | 180 |
| 3 | 260 |

Would a dot plot with one dot per visitor be a practical display? Explain your answer.
examples.solution_text:
No. Although the numbers of books are numerical counts, the frequencies would require hundreds of dots. The dot plot would be crowded and slow to draw and read.

A **column graph** could show the three book counts and their frequencies more clearly.

coverage.summary: Added six worked examples covering all six distinct assessed methods, with one mapping for each of the 21 assessment locators. Adaptations use different contexts and values and keep Stage 3 language and mathematics. Questions and solutions are separate editable fields; solution prose inherits the renderer's blue. Tables provide the necessary data without revealing the chosen display. No equation gutters or diagram annotations are needed for these selection tasks. examples.derivation: Cycling, swimming and walking are named categories. Separate columns with heights 9, 12 and 6 allow comparison. A column graph is suitable; construction is not requested.
Heights 8, 11, 15 and 18 cm are measurements at consecutive weeks. A line graph with week horizontally and height vertically shows change over time, matching the source method.

The parks are named categories, so intermediate positions between their names have no defined meaning. Joining counts is inappropriate for this comparison; separate columns represent 6, 10 and 8 birds.

There are 24 choices: apple represents one half, banana one quarter and orange one quarter. A sector graph directly represents these shares of the whole. No fraction calculation is required of the learner.
One picture per item requires 150 + 230 + 320 = 700 drawings. Three columns provide a practical comparison. An even scale from 0 to 350 in steps of 50 accommodates the maximum value, 320.
One dot per visitor requires 120 + 180 + 260 = 560 dots. The book counts are numerical, but these frequencies make the proposed display impractical. Three columns can show the frequencies clearly.
